turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, come in and sit down. You look a bit washed out, hey. What's been going on?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doctor, I don't even know where to start, so I'll just talk. I'm thirty-eight, I stay with my sister in Yeoville, and I work at the clothing shop in Rosebank, on my feet from eight until five. The thing is I'm tired, properly finished tired, and my periods have become hectic. I get home, I lie on the couch, I don't even put the soapie on.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That sounds really draining. How long have you been feeling this tired?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it, that's the annoying part. It crept up on me. Maybe it was around when the periods changed, but I couldn't tell you the month, never mind the week. It's worse after a long shift, when we've had a sale and I'm folding jerseys till closing.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Tell me about the periods, in as much detail as you like. What's different from before?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): They've been heavy for six months... no, wait, that's wrong. My birthday is in March and last year it was already like this, so it's a year, a full year. They used to be four easy days. Now the whole thing goes on for nine days... actually ten, I said nine but it's ten, I counted on the calendar on the fridge, and they pitch every three weeks, early, so I'm never ready with pads.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you say heavy, how many pads do you go through, and do you pass clots?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I lose count, truly. On the bad days it's the whole pack of the thick night ones, the big purple packet from the chemist, and I'm changing the whole time, at work I have to leave the floor between customers. There are clots as well, big ones, about the size of a R5 coin, sometimes bigger, like a bottle top, I can't give you a proper number. It's just a lot, and I'm sorry I'm rambling.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise, this is exactly what I need. Any shortness of breath, or pain in the chest?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathless, ja. Our lift is broken again, with the load shedding the building just gives up, so I walk to the third floor and I'm huffing like I ran for the taxi. Chest pain, no. Nothing like that, my chest doesn't hurt at all.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does that breathlessness happen while you're sitting still, or only when you're on the go?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Only when I'm doing something. Sitting I'm alright. Stairs, the taxi rank, even hanging the washing on the balcony, I'm out of breath. At night I'm fine, I sleep ok, I don't wake up gasping or anything.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or fever, that sort of thing?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. No fever, I checked with my sister's thermometer last week because she was convinced, and it was normal. I do feel cold in the shop but that's the aircon, it's arctic in there, my colleague wears a jersey too, so I don't think it's me.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): And dizziness, or any fainting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No, I don't get dizzy, and I've never fainted. I'm steady on my feet, even on those stairs.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your hair or your skin? People sometimes notice changes when the periods are like this.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the hair. In the shower it comes out in clumps, I have to pull it out of the drain every single time, and my ponytail is much thinner than it used to be. I blamed the cheap shampoo from the chemist, so I went back to my old one, the one in the green bottle, and it's still falling. My sister saw it on the bathroom floor before I even admitted it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines at the moment, even something you only use now and then?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the iron. The clinic sister put me on ferrous sulphate, seventy-five milligrams... no, sorry, I always get that wrong, the bottle says two hundred milligrams. Twice a day, by mouth, because she said my iron was low, for the tiredness and the periods. But I only take it sometimes, hey, it makes my stomach a bit off so I skip it, or I just forget, maybe three times in a week if I'm being good.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the dose on the bottle is two hundred milligrams twice a day, and most days it's not actually going in.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, exactly. Some weeks even less than that. I park the bottle next to the kettle so I'll see it when I make tea, and I still walk right past it. I feel bad about it, the sister was very firm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets, and any allergies to medicines or anything else?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No other tablets. I'm not on the pill or anything. Allergies, no, nothing I know of. I had penicillin for a tooth a few years back and I was completely fine, no rash, no swelling.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about illnesses in the family? Anything your people tend to get?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom has an underactive thyroid. She's been on treatment for years, the little white tablets, I don't know the name. My auntie is always saying thyroid runs in our family, she phones me about it whenever someone is tired. My dad, I think he might have blood pressure, but he doesn't talk about his health, so I can't swear to that.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's worth knowing. Any bleeding between the periods, or spotting?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No spotting in between, it stays in its lane, just heavy when it comes. And before you ask, I'm not seeing anyone at the moment, we broke up in winter, his mother never liked me, long story, so there's nothing after sex to report. Otherwise the cycle is just early and long, like I said.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed, or your appetite?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Weight is the same, my work skirt still fits, which is something. Appetite is fine, I eat. Pap and veg most nights, sometimes chicken if it's on special at Shoprite. I don't skip meals, my sister would have a word with me if I did.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your bowels, and passing water? Any trouble there?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine, no diarrhoea, no constipation, regular as anything. Wee is normal, no burning, no running to the toilet. I do drink a lot of water at work because the shop is warm once they switch the aircon off, but that's just habit, not because of a problem.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take alcohol?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, not even at varsity. Alcohol, ja, a glass of wine at a braai, not every weekend, just when my sister's husband makes chops. Last Saturday the power went in the middle of it and we finished on the gas cooker, but that's not a health thing, sorry.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, you're fine, I like the full picture. I'm going to have a look at you now, and I'll talk you through it.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. My hands are cold, sorry, that's the waiting room, the fan is right above the chairs. The magazine was from 2019, can you believe.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're a bit pale in the inner eyelids. Chest is clear, no wheeze, heart sounds are normal with no murmur, and your tummy is soft and not tender. Blood pressure is one hundred and eighteen over seventy-six, pulse ninety-six, oxygen ninety-eight percent, and you're breathing at sixteen.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-six bad? I get nervous when people count things on me. At the shop they count the takings and I also get nervous, which is silly, it's not even my money.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a bit quicker than I'd like, but not dangerous on its own. It fits with you being run down. Is there anything you nearly didn't mention, something you brushed off earlier?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, well, actually, ja. I said I don't get dizzy, and that's not quite true. Last week at Shoprite I bent down for the mielie meal, and when I stood up the whole aisle went grey and I had to hold the trolley. It's happened a few times when I stand up too fast. I didn't fall, but it wasn't nothing.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you came back to that. How often, and have you actually collapsed?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Not collapsed, no, I've never ended up on the floor. Three or four times this past month, only when I get up quickly, and it passes in a few seconds. The Shoprite one was the worst because the queue was behind me and I felt stupid standing there clinging to a trolley.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, I think the most likely thing is iron deficiency anaemia from these heavy periods. I can't confirm it until we see the bloods. With your mom's thyroid, an underactive thyroid is also possible and I wouldn't rule it out, but that's not my first thought.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I need a scan? My friend Nomsa had fibroids and they only found them on a scan, she bled for ages, and now I'm wondering if that's me, even though I know you can't say from the outside.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll do bloods today, a full blood count, a ferritin, and a thyroid test. A pelvic scan we might arrange if the bloods show you're very anaemic, or if the bleeding carries on this heavy. I'm not booking the scan today.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I hate needles, I'll warn you. In 2019 a student at the clinic dug around in my arm for ages and I nearly cried in front of the whole waiting room, so I get tense, but I'll do it. Just tell them to use the good vein, the left one.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): They'll be gentle. Please start taking that iron properly, two hundred milligrams twice a day, with food, and have it with orange juice rather than tea. If you're soaking a pad every hour, or you faint, or you get chest pain or much worse breathlessness, don't wait, come straight in.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. With food, not tea, I can do that, and if I'm soaking through or I feel faint I'll come in, I won't be brave about it. Orange juice is fine, we buy the two litre. When do I hear about the results?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through them together. I'll ask reception to book you on your way out.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is fine. My sister might come with me, she likes to hear things herself because I leave bits out, which, ja, I just did with the dizziness. We'll be here.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the hair worrying you as much as the bleeding, or is there something else on your mind?

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): The hair, ja. I keep comparing photos of my ponytail from the December braai and it looks half the thickness, and I know photos lie with the light, but still. Will it grow back, or is this just how I am now?

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): If this is the iron, hair often settles once the levels come up, but I don't want to promise that before the tests. We'll know more in two weeks, and we'll take it from there.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still work? I can't really take off, the shop is short-staffed and my manager already gave me a look when I asked for this morning. I'll stand if you say it's safe.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep working, and sit when you can, and don't skip meals. If the stairs become too much and you're properly breathless, phone us sooner rather than pushing through to the two weeks.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, I'll keep working then, I'll sit when I can, and I won't skip meals. I'll take the iron properly, and I'll buy pads on the way home. If the stairs get too much I'll phone you, I promise. Thank you, hey, I feel less all over the place, and I'll see you in two weeks.
